items.title: The family-tree method (draw it, don't guess)
items.body:
### Drawing the family tree

**The idea in one sentence**
Turn every blood-relation sentence into a small top-down diagram so that gender and generation are fixed on paper instead of juggled in your head.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Take "X is the father of Y; Y is the sister of Z." Build it one piece at a time:
```
        X  (male, father)
        |
   +----+----+
   Y         Z
 (female)
```
X is on top. Y and Z share the same parent X, so they sit on the row below, joined as siblings. Y is female (a sister). Since X is the father of Y and Z is Y's sibling, X is also the father of Z. Reading the finished picture gives the answer directly, with no guessing.

**Why draw instead of reasoning in your head?**
Because across three or four links the mind loses track of who is male or female and which generation they are in; a drawing pins both down so a careless slip becomes almost impossible.

**Picture**
```
elders        -> top row
their children-> next row down
same generation sits on one row
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| square | male |
| circle | female |
| horizontal line | a married couple |
| vertical line | parent down to child |
| bracket below two names | siblings (same parents) |

**The formula or method**
Read the sentence in small pieces, fix each gender the instant a gendered word appears, place elders on top and children below, then read the answer from the target person's point of view.

**Exam-level example**
"A is B's sister; C is B's mother; D is C's father. How is A related to D?"
1. Put D on top; C (D's child) below D; then A and B below C.
2. A is female and sits two descent steps below D.
3. Two steps down from a person is a grandchild, so A is D's **granddaughter**. Check: D→C is one step (parent), C→A is the second (grandparent), and A is female. ✓

**Common traps**
- Inventing a spouse or extra sibling the sentence never mentions.
- Reading the relation from the wrong person's side.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| elders on top, children below | one generation per row |
| fix gender at once | square male, circle female |
| read from the target | answer "how is A related to D" from A's side |
keyPoints: Draw a top-down tree: elders on top, children below, same generation on one row.
Square = male, circle = female, horizontal line = married couple, vertical line = parent to child.
Fix gender the instant a gendered word (son, daughter, wife, brother) appears.
Read the answer from the target person's point of view.
Do not invent siblings or spouses that the statement never mentions.

items.title: Decoding coded (symbol) blood relations
items.body:
### Decoding symbol (coded) relations

**The idea in one sentence**
Symbols such as +, −, ×, ÷ stand for relationships, and you read a chain one link at a time, writing each link as a plain sentence before drawing it.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Suppose "A × B" means "A is the father of B" and "A ÷ B" means "A is the daughter of B". Decode "P × Q ÷ R":
```
P × Q  ->  P is father of Q
Q ÷ R  ->  Q is daughter of R   (so R is Q's parent)

        R
        |
   P -- (parent) -- Q   both are Q's parents
```
P is Q's father. Q is R's daughter, so R is Q's other parent, meaning R is Q's mother. Two parents of the same child are married, so P is R's husband.

**Why translate each link into a sentence first?**
Because the symbol hides the direction; writing "A is the father of B" forces you to notice who is above whom before you draw, which is exactly where candidates slip.

**Picture**
```
legend:  A × B = A is father of B
         A ÷ B = A is daughter of B
chain:   P × Q ÷ R   read left to right
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| the key | the question's table of which symbol is which relation |
| link | one pair joined by a symbol, like A × B |
| chain | several links sharing a middle person |

**The formula or method**
Write the key as a legend, translate each link into "A is the (relation) of B", join links so the shared person connects them, then read the asked relation and its direction.

**Exam-level example**
Key as above; decode "P × Q ÷ R" and find how P relates to R.
1. P × Q means P is Q's father.
2. Q ÷ R means Q is R's daughter, so R is Q's mother.
3. P and R are both parents of Q, so they are spouses; P is R's **husband**. Check: swapping gives R is P's wife, consistent. ✓

**Common traps**
- Reaching a person through the father (paternal) but labelling it maternal, or the reverse.
- Answering the natural chain direction when the question asks the reverse ("how is R related to P").

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| legend first | note every symbol's relation |
| one link, one sentence | "A is the __ of B" |
| two parents of one child | they are spouses |
keyPoints: Write the symbol legend first, then translate each link to 'A is the __ of B'.
Join links so the second person of one link is the first of the next.
A route through the father gives a paternal relative; through the mother, a maternal relative.
Two people who are both parents of one child are spouses.
Watch the asked direction: father-in-law and son-in-law are opposite ends of the same link.

items.title: Pointing & photograph statements — resolve the self-reference
items.body:
### Pointing-at-a-photograph statements

**The idea in one sentence**
A speaker describes someone through a chain that often loops back to the speaker, so your first job is to spot the clause that secretly names the speaker.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Take Latha saying of a man, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother." Work the inner phrase first:
```
my mother's only daughter = Latha herself
(a mother with one daughter can only mean the speaker)
so  the man's mother = Latha
            Latha
             |
            man
```
Replace "the only daughter of my mother" with "Latha". Then "the man's mother is Latha" means Latha is the man's mother. Collapsing the self-referring clause turns a confusing sentence into a one-line relation.

**Why replace the clause with the speaker?**
Because a phrase like "the only daughter of my mother" is a disguised way of saying "me"; until you swap it for the speaker, the rest of the sentence cannot be read cleanly.

**Picture**
```
"the only daughter of my mother"  -> the female speaker
"the only son of my father"       -> the male speaker
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| self-referring clause | a roundabout phrase that names the speaker |
| resolve | replace that clause with the word "speaker" |

**The formula or method**
Work the phrase from the inside outward, replace any clause that circles back to the speaker with "speaker", then read the leftover relation.

**Exam-level example**
A man points to a boy and says, "He is the son of my only son." How is the boy related to the man?
1. "My only son" is the man's son.
2. "The son of my only son" is that son's son.
3. So the boy is the man's **grandson**. Check: two descent steps below the man, and male, so grandson. ✓

**Common traps**
- Reading "the only daughter of my mother" as the speaker's sister rather than the speaker.
- Resolving the outer phrase before the inner one and losing the thread.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| collapse the self-reference | "only daughter of my mother" is the female speaker |
| inside-out | resolve the innermost phrase first |
keyPoints: Collapse self-referring clauses first: 'only daughter of my mother' is the female speaker.
'Only son of my father' said by a man is the man himself.
Work the phrase inside-out, then read the leftover relation.
The speaker's gender is revealed by 'daughter' or 'son' but not by the neutral word 'child'.

items.title: Data sufficiency in blood relations — the gender check
items.body:
### Data sufficiency — the gender check

**The idea in one sentence**
A data-sufficiency item asks only whether the statements are enough to fix a relation, not what the relation is, and the usual gap is a missing gender.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Take: "How is M related to N? Statement I: M is the child of N. Statement II: N is the mother of two children." Test each alone, then together:
```
I alone:  N --+-- ?        M is a child of N, but son or daughter? unknown
              M
II alone: tells N has two children, nothing about M
I + II:   N is mother; M is one child, still son OR daughter
```
Even with both statements the tree is complete but the son-versus-daughter gender is still open, so the exact relation cannot be named — the data is not sufficient.

**Why is a complete tree still not enough?**
Because "child" is gender-neutral; you can place M correctly and still not know whether M is a son or a daughter, and the asked relation needs that gender.

**Picture**
```
tree fixed?  yes
gender fixed? no  -> relation still undecided
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| statement I / II | the two clues, each tested on its own first |
| sufficient | the clue(s) pin down the exact relation |
| gender-neutral word | child, parent, cousin, sibling, spouse |

**The formula or method**
Test statement I alone, then II alone, then both together; before calling anything sufficient, check the target person's gender is fixed.

**Exam-level example**
"Is M male or female? Statement: M is the son of N."
1. Read the statement: the word "son" is given.
2. "Son" fixes M as male on its own.
3. So the single statement is **sufficient**. Check: no other gender reading of "son" exists. ✓

**Common traps**
- Declaring a statement sufficient while a needed gender is still unknown.
- Combining the two statements before testing each one alone.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| test I, then II, then both | each clue alone first |
| tree complete ≠ relation fixed | a missing gender still blocks the answer |
keyPoints: Data sufficiency asks whether the relation is determinable, not what it is.
Test statement I alone, then II alone, then both together.
Always verify the target person's gender is fixed before declaring sufficiency.
'Child', 'parent', 'cousin', 'spouse' are gender-neutral traps.
A statement can fix the family tree yet be insufficient for lack of a gender.

items.title: Common traps: 'only', maternal vs paternal, and generations
items.body:
Three recurring tricks decide most hard relation questions: the word "only", the maternal-versus-paternal side, and miscounting generations. Each is a method to apply, not just a warning.

### Maternal versus paternal, and counting generations

**The idea in one sentence**
The same label (uncle, grandfather) is maternal or paternal depending on the route you took, and the generation name depends on how many parent-to-child steps you counted.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Take "A is the father of F; F is the father of B; B is the mother of C. How is A related to C?" Count the descent links down the drawn chain:
```
A  (father)
|
F  (father)
|
B  (mother)
|
C
```
From A to C there are three downward steps: A→F, F→B, B→C. One step down is a parent, two is a grandparent, three is a great-grandparent. A is male, so A is C's great-grandfather.

**Why count the links instead of naming by feel?**
Because "grandfather" and "great-grandfather" feel similar, but they differ by exactly one generation; counting the parent-to-child steps removes the guess.

**Picture**
```
links down: 1 = parent, 2 = grandparent, 3 = great-grandparent
maternal = reached via the mother; paternal = via the father
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| descent link | one parent-to-child step |
| maternal | reached through the mother's side |
| paternal | reached through the father's side |

**The formula or method**
Count the descent links to name the generation (1 parent, 2 grandparent, 3 great-grandparent), and trace whether you passed through the mother (maternal) or the father (paternal).

**Exam-level example**
Using the chain above, how is A related to C?
1. Steps A→F→B→C number three.
2. Three steps down is a great-grandparent.
3. A is male, so A is C's **great-grandfather**. Check: stopping at B would wrongly give "grandfather"; the third step matters. ✓

**Common traps**
- Dropping one generation and calling a great-grandparent a grandparent.
- Treating a maternal uncle and a paternal uncle as the same when the side is asked.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| count descent links | 1 parent, 2 grandparent, 3 great-grandparent |
| track the route | maternal via mother, paternal via father |

### The word "only" and in-law directions

**The idea in one sentence**
"Only son" or "only daughter" forces a single identity on that side, and in-law relations flip depending on which end of a marriage link you are asked about.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Take "R is the only son of S." Draw S with R as the sole son:
```
        S
        |
       R   (the ONLY son)
```
Because R is the only son, there is no other son of S anywhere in the puzzle; so any later phrase like "S's son" must be R himself. The word "only" has quietly removed every rival branch, which collapses the puzzle.

**Why does "only" matter so much?**
Because it rules out cousins, extra sons, or extra daughters on that side; without it a phrase like "S's son" could be any number of people, but with it there is exactly one.

**Picture**
```
spouse's parent  = parent-in-law
daughter's husband = son-in-law
(opposite ends of ONE marriage link)
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| only | there is exactly one person of that kind |
| parent-in-law | the parent of one's spouse |
| son-in-law | the husband of one's daughter |

**The formula or method**
When you see "only", delete any cousin, aunt or uncle branch on that side; for in-laws, decide which end of the marriage link the question asks before naming it.

**Exam-level example**
"R is the only son of S" — later the puzzle says "S's son went to market." Who went?
1. S has only one son, R.
2. So "S's son" cannot be anyone else.
3. **R** went to market. Check: no other son exists, so there is no ambiguity. ✓

**Common traps**
- Allowing a second son or a cousin when "only" has ruled them out.
- Confusing a parent-in-law with a child-in-law, which sit at opposite ends of a marriage.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| "only" removes rivals | exactly one person of that kind |
| in-laws have a direction | re-read which end is asked |
keyPoints: 'Only son' or 'only daughter' blocks cousin, aunt and uncle branches on that side.
The same label (uncle, aunt, grandfather) is maternal or paternal by the route taken.
Descent links up: 1 is parent, 2 is grandparent, 3 is great-grandparent.
A spouse's parent is a parent-in-law; a daughter's husband is a son-in-law (opposite ends).
Re-read which direction the question asks before finalising the answer.

items.title: Seating arrangement & ranking — the counting formulas
items.body:
The same paper mixes relations with seating and ranking puzzles. Each is solved by drawing the positions and using one counting rule, below.

### Ranking in a line (counting from both ends)

**The idea in one sentence**
When a person is counted from both ends of a line, the person is counted twice, so the total is the two counts added and then one subtracted.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Ravi is 7th from the left and 12th from the right. Draw the line and mark Ravi once:
```
L 1 2 3 4 5 6 [R] . . . . . . . . . .  R-end
          7th from left, 12th from right
left of Ravi: 6   Ravi: 1   right of Ravi: 11
total = 6 + 1 + 11 = 18
```
Adding the two counts gives 7 + 12 = 19, but Ravi himself has been counted in both the 7 and the 12, so subtract that one duplicate: 19 − 1 = 18.

**Why subtract one and not zero or two?**
Because exactly one person — Ravi — appears in both counts; the people to his left and right are each counted once, only he is counted twice.

**Picture**
```
left count + right count counts the shared person twice
total = left + right - 1
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| from the left / right | the position counted from that end |
| total | how many people are in the line |

**The formula or method**
Total people = (position from left) + (position from right) − 1; and position from the other end = total − (position from this end) + 1.

**Exam-level example**
In a row of 40, which position from the right is the 16th from the left?
1. Position from the other end = 40 − 16 + 1 = 25th from the right.
2. Check with the line rule: 16 + 25 − 1 = 40.
3. So it is the **25th from the right**. The common slip is writing 40 − 16 = 24 and forgetting the + 1. ✓

**Common traps**
- Forgetting the − 1, so the shared person is counted twice.
- Dropping the + 1 when converting a position to the other end.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| total = left + right − 1 | subtract the double-counted person |
| left + right = total + 1 | any one follows from the other two |

### Seating in a row (facing direction)

**The idea in one sentence**
In a straight row the "left" and "right" of a person depend on which way they face, so you must set the facing direction before placing neighbours.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Suppose five friends face north and P is in the middle with Q to P's immediate right. Draw them as you look at a north-facing row (their left is your left):
```
your view:  _  _  P  Q  _
            L1 L2    (P's right = your right)
```
For a north-facing person, their left and right match yours. For a south-facing person they would be swapped: their right is on your left. Fixing the facing first stops every left/right mistake.

**Why does facing change left and right?**
Because a person's own left hand points opposite ways depending on whether they look towards you (south-facing) or away (north-facing); their left is not always your left.

**Picture**
```
north-facing: their left = your left
south-facing: their left = your right (swapped)
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| north-facing | looking away from you; left/right match yours |
| south-facing | looking towards you; left/right are swapped |

**The formula or method**
Fix the most definite clue first (often a middle or end seat); for a north-facing row keep left and right as you see them, for a south-facing row swap them.

**Exam-level example**
In a north-facing row, Q sits immediately to the right of P. On your diagram, where is Q?
1. The row faces north, so their right equals your right.
2. "Immediate right of P" is one seat to your right of P.
3. Q is the **seat just to the right of P** as you look at it. Check: if they faced south, Q would instead be on your left. ✓

**Common traps**
- Not swapping left and right for a south-facing row.
- Placing a neighbour before fixing a definite anchor seat.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| set the facing first | north keeps, south swaps |
| anchor the sure seat | build neighbours out from it |

### Seating in a circle

**The idea in one sentence**
Around a circle people face the centre and the seats loop, so a chain of "immediate right" clues eventually returns to the first person, and the seat opposite is half the circle away.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Six people A to F sit around a circle, each facing the centre, with each named to the immediate right of the one before. Place them going clockwise:
```
        A
    F       B
    E       C
        D
```
Follow "immediate right" clues around until the last person sits beside the first again. Here A's opposite is D, three seats away, because half of six is three.

**Why does the opposite seat work only for an even number?**
Because "directly opposite" needs the circle to split into two equal halves; with an odd number of seats no seat sits exactly across from another.

**Picture**
```
n seats, facing centre
seat opposite = n/2 places away (only when n is even)
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| facing the centre | each person's left and right are set towards the middle |
| opposite seat | the seat directly across the circle |

**The formula or method**
Follow the immediate-right (or left) chain around the loop; for an even number of seats the opposite person is n/2 places away, and "k to the left" equals "(n − k) to the right".

**Exam-level example**
In a circle of 6 facing the centre, who sits opposite the 1st person?
1. Half of 6 is 3.
2. Count 3 seats around from the 1st person.
3. The person **3 seats away** sits opposite. Check: with 6 seats the circle splits into two halves of 3, so this is exact. ✓

**Common traps**
- Using the opposite-seat rule when the number of seats is odd.
- Mixing clockwise and anticlockwise when following the chain.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| chain the right-neighbour clues | the loop returns to the first |
| opposite = n/2 away | only when n is even |
keyPoints: Total from both ends = left count + right count − 1 (subtract the double-counted person).
Position from the other end = total − (position from this end) + 1.
Fix the most-constrained seat first; north-facing keeps your left, south-facing swaps it.
In a circle, 'k to the left' equals '(n − k) to the right'; the opposite seat is half of n away when n is even.
'k places below rank r' is rank (r + k) from the top; on an interchange each takes the other's seat.

items.title: Multi-step chained relation riddles
items.body:
### Multi-step chained relation riddles

**The idea in one sentence**
A single sentence chains three or four relation links, and you unpack it from the innermost phrase outward, drawing each link on a tree.

**Do it the slow way first (draw it)**
Take "P is the mother of A's brother's father's wife." Start from the phrase deepest inside, closest to the name:
```
A's brother's father = A's own father   (siblings share a father)
A's father's wife    = A's mother
P is the mother of A's mother:

        P  (maternal grandmother)
        |
      A's mother
        |
        A
```
So P is the mother of A's mother, which makes P the maternal grandmother of A. Resolving one layer at a time keeps the chain from tangling.

**Why resolve the innermost phrase first?**
Because each outer phrase depends on the one inside it; if you start from the outside you have nothing fixed to attach it to, and the links collapse into confusion.

**Picture**
```
innermost -> next -> next -> whole
A's brother's father | 's wife | P is the mother of __
```

**What the symbols mean**
| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| innermost phrase | the possessive closest to a name |
| maternal | on the mother's side |

**The formula or method**
Find the innermost possessive phrase and name the person it points to, replace it and step one layer outward, fixing each gender as you go, then read the final relation.

**Exam-level example**
"A's brother's father" — who is this?
1. The innermost phrase is "A's brother".
2. That brother's father is the same man who is A's father, because siblings share a father.
3. So "A's brother's father" is simply **A's father**. Check: a brother and A have the same parents. ✓

**Common traps**
- Treating "A's brother's father" as a brand-new man rather than A's own father.
- Resolving the outer phrase before the inner one and losing track.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| inside-out | resolve the innermost phrase first |
| mother of the mother | maternal grandmother |
keyPoints: Resolve chained riddles innermost-phrase-first, one link at a time.
'A's brother's father' is A's father; 'father's wife' is the mother.
The mother of A's mother is A's maternal grandmother.
'Only granddaughter of a maternal great-grandfather' is the mother.
'Maternal' fixes the mother's side; 'only' forces a unique identity.
